author: hoeschec
text:
I have been a silent reader of this forum for several months and decided to start a Journal and begin contributing to this wonderful community. I'd like to thank IF for offering this place to those of us who are committed to understanding how and why the market moves like it does. I am immensely thankful for the time and continued efforts all associate and master traders who take the time to respond to those of us who are still in the beginning stages of our journey to becoming competent traders.

I found this website in August 2014 and joined November 2014. Despite not posting any content to date, I have spent at least an hour a day going through the homework assignments and member journals in my quest to understand price movement. Previous to finding RTM last year I spent two arduous years trading Forex with little success. This community has helped tremendously.

I have read through all of the materials posted under the Marketpedia section (multiple times) and after reading through various Journals over several months I feel the following concepts are most important when it comes to truly understanding how everything fits together: It has something to do with the relationship between:

1. How to accurately draw all price action zones and understand the difference between an engulf and a fakeout. 2. Proficiency in using multiple time frames to utilize the fractal nature of the market to pinpoint critical reaction levels and decision points.

Aaron's 'Homework Room' topic titled 'Engulf or Fakeout?' has been a great resource that has helped me see the difference between an engulf/fakeout. Many thanks to him for starting that thread!

For me, drawing the PAZ is the most challenging concept to understand and draw accurately. My goal is to finally take each article from the Marketpedia section and begin combining the concepts together to see the bigger picture behind price movement. This journal will be a great place to begin this journey, post my charts, and track my progress.

I plan on posting both historical chart analysis (hindsight) for conceptual purposes as well as live trades taken on a demo account for practical application and accountability. I will perform a 'trade autopsy' on any live trades I take that fail so I can identify the mistakes and eliminate bad habits.

First chart posted here is just for practice to make sure I am inserting the picture correctly. I am using Gyazo to snap screenshots.

More posts to follow...

author: hoeschec
text:
Trade Setup – Hindsight: I found a nice example of an AUD/USD FTB reaction that took place back on 6/2/15. This is not a trade I caught in real time but one I researched in hindsight to see if I could identify why price reacted like it did.

HTF Analysis: This is a good area to look for a reaction on the FTB because the associated FTR is significant. There is a clear decision made that price is too expensive and a resulting price cap is formed. There is a strong bearish move out of the FTR showing a significant imbalance where more orders may exist when price returns to this area. Because of these factors, I will watch the 4-hour chart until price reaches the FTR zone, at which point I will drop down to a LTF to look for specific price action to make an entry.

LTF Analysis: Price moves up through the lower limit of the FTR. Since I know price is returning for the first time, I am looking for a reason to short. Primarily, I am focused on price forming an engulf to the downside before considering any entry. This is not a situation where I would risk a TT.

In this example, price does end up engulfing and in doing so also forms the LL of the QM.

I labeled the source of the engulf as the location where I would have executed a short trade. I would have placed a stop just above the upper limit of the FTR (around.78420). Target is shown on chart. My target might be a little aggressive, and there’s a good chance I would have taken ½ of the position off around.76940 just to be safe.

Fakeout vs Engulf: It’s my understanding that price will fakeout when IT’s needs orders. Fakeouts are used to push price in to a specific zone that will contain orders. Engulfs and fakeouts both have the same effect on retail traders (tricks), but the engulf is really just indicative of future price direction. Because of this, engulfs usually don’t engulf in to a significant level. That is why I think this example shows an engulf and not a F/O.

author: hoeschec
text:
This is an example on EUR/GBP (4-HR Chart) where compression exists between two FTR’s. My focus is on the location of the engulf and the subsequent final bullish push through the CP in to the FTR zone above (by the large black arrow).

Was there a way I could have predicted that price would reach the upper FTR following the bearish engulf?

I am not entirely sure how to read this chart accurately. On one hand, the engulf on the 4-hour chart could be read as a clear intention for price to drop. In this were case, the IT’s would need to fill lots of short orders. Since the lower FTR zone is depleted (three times price has visited this FTR), it would make logical sense that price would need to find the next real level of Supply to fill short orders. The push through the CP to the upper FTR could be seen as a FTB, but it also looks like a great place to FO and load up on short orders.

Maybe this is both a FTB and a FO?

IF’s trades often occur at levels where he experiences very little (if any) drawdown. After breaking down some of those amazing trades I notice many times he is able to predict in advance and place a PO at the exact area where price turns.

I could be wrong, but it seems like he knows where the fakeouts will occur by looking left of the engulf to see what the RBD/ DBR (supply/demand) is reacting to (usually an important FTR) and determining whether there are any extreme orders left to fill in that FTR. If so, price will likely FO to a specific decision point within this FTR. That is why he often drop down to a 5 minute or 1 minute chart to plot his entry….he is looking for the most accurate decision point.

This is what I need to work on because trading at these extreme levels offers the highest R:R.

author: hoeschec
text:
One of my worst habits is being overly anxious to get in a trade out of fear that I'll miss an opportunity. It's a completely irrational fear, as any trader knows there are dozens of prime setups that occur every day. That said, I still regularly fall victim to this and it happened this evening on a trade I took on the Cable. Here are the charts (1-HR and 1-Min)

I saw price bounce from a HTF FTR, so I dropped down to a 1-minute chart to see price action. The 1-minute chat showed a nice engulf and bearish QM setup so I waited for price to retrace to the origin of the engulf and took a short trade. My stop was a couple of pips above the swing high and my target was the base of the pole.

Here is why it went wrong:

Almost as soon as I executed the short trade I began having doubts. I looked at the 4-HR chart and saw a bullish reaction out of demand which made me question my reasons for taking short. Even though the short position was a quick scalp, I was concerned the QM was going to fail. Because of this, I closed the trade with a minimal 2.5 pip gain (barely enough to cover the spread).

Of course, within a few short minutes of closing my position, price ended up dropping to easily hit my original target. I tried to jump back in when I saw price take a dive, but was only able to pick up another 4 or 5 pips.

I am embarrassed to admit that after three years of trading I still make these kind of mistakes.

Looking forward to kicking this bad habit.

author: hoeschec
text:
Here is a follow up from my AUD/USD Chart from last week (see Post #2 for original post on this pair).

I listed the steps (see chart) that I would take when watching price develop in to this critical level to predict a F/O. In this case, price did react nicely to this level, as it picked up the extreme set of orders still left in the original FTR. My question: it it OK that price (when forming "A") exceeded the extreme set of orders by a few pips (see the orange dotted line)? If so, why did this happen and how can I predict this happening in the future? I don't see any value in pushing price beyond the last set of orders in the FTR, unless it was done just to fool traders. Even so, this ~ 10 pip move past the extreme FTR seems arbitrary.

When IF takes his trades, he seems to know almost exactly where price will turn. While I am not expecting to trade with IF's level of accuracy, it does concern me when an extreme level (which is supposed to be a F/O) is engulfed. It makes me think I am misreading the chart.

Of course, ideally a trader would zoom in and watch for PA before taking a trade. That said, IF has many trades that he takes without waiting for price action because he is expecting the F/O and knows exactly where price will turn. This is what I am trying to understand on a conceptual level.

author: hoeschec
text:
Thanks for the reality check and encouragement Ptp!! Maybe I am getting caught up on insignificant details (I have a tendency to obsess on details and miss the main point). Where I often struggle is stop placement - either the trades get run through or the stop gets hit just before price reverses. The difference between a winning trade and a losing trade can be stop placement.

Knowing price is going to F/O allows a trader to widen their stop and keeps them on the right side of R:R. It's amazing to see how bad timing on an otherwise excellent trade setup can take a major winner and turn it in to a loser. I am actually embarrassed at how often my stops get hit...

To improve on my past errors, I have started closely watching price to understand why price changes when it does. That's why I was surprised to see price break the extreme orders of the FTR by ten pips (AUD/USD).

IF has mentioned many times that predicting a F/O should be easy. I agree that an engulf or a F/O have basically the same effect on retail traders as far as trapping them on the wrong side of the trade (and in that context the difference between them really doesn't matter). Of course, the difference between the engulf and F/O is the engulf dictates future price direction. And I would suggest (from what I know as a beginner) that it is incredibly important to distinguish between the two from a practical perspective.

I suppose the other aspect of this that I need to work on is the PAZ. It seems simple enough in theory...PAZ is just the space between FTR's. For some reason, once I open a live chart, I start getting all mixed up on how to draw them, how to not leave any out, and how to understand price's reaction to them.

Enough of my rambling...I really appreciate that you and D took the time to leave a comment here and I will try to stay focused on the bigger picture and get really competent at specific setups that I can duplicate over and over.

You have the right attitude which is more important than any price structure. In the trade of #19, my advice is to try to avoid looking for the exact reason. Is price at a key supply/SR zone? Check. First time back? Check. If you want to, was there an engulf? Check. Now decide where to get in. If you see the RBD between the doji and the red candle, theres a clear little pullback in there - one of those "ftr" things. Its simply a pullback before the drop, and theres a level in it. That little ftr is NO DIFFERENT to a fakeout, its just within the price curve it was part of in the up move. I dont even know whats left but that push up had to react at the most obvious next reaction point, which is the FTR or whatver its called.....and to be clear, I would have been in on the RBD, not the retest, around 27722 or even around 277738. This was a really easy trade H - so if it feels like it is hard, you are possibly looking for something thats not there, or really not relevant. This trade is at major supply, and it rotates. Jump in on the rotation or wait for the engulf. If you look at the M1 chart at the PA left of the entry, what I see as being more predictive is a nice SR level around the entry. If you look at M1 the entry higher, simple SR, was a much better price. In either case you still dont know if price will rip north...thats the uncertainty principle. I personally dont like the entry that was taken - it looks good on a H1.

Nick.
